requirement:
Habeas MUST provide the built-in `habeas:coverage` under
{cite}`requirements.references.builtin_definitions`, with this text:

> Cite this on a source file or explicitly declared function to propose a
> coverage exception. Explain in prose why the item's incomplete execution
> coverage is acceptable. Put the explanation in fenced citation commentary
> or Rust doc comments included in the source item's assessed input. An ordinary
> non-doc comment alone does not supply a tracked justification. The reason
> must be substantive; difficulty alone is not a justification.
> On a file's root item, the exception excuses only
> that file's 80% instrumented-line threshold, including absent measurement
> of its executable code. On an explicit function with a body, it excuses
> that function's recorded zero execution or absence from otherwise usable
> measurement, without excusing the file's threshold.
> The explanation must agree with the current source and any callers or
> configuration assumptions on which it relies. Only a current accepted
> independent assessment permits the exception. A file exception does not
> excuse unexecuted or not-measured functions in that file.
> The citation applies to its source item without conditional build matching
> and may remain when measured coverage satisfies the item's obligations.

Only `{cite}` MAY reference this built-in, inline or fenced using the standard
reference forms of {cite}`requirements.references.roles`. The built-in MUST be
available in every project without a project requirement, site query, or
exception-specific configuration.
rationale:
structural: `requirements.test-coverage.check.exceptions.anchor` has no structural obligations, and it has no implementation edges or roots. I checked each clause for one.

- **"Habeas MUST provide the built-in `habeas:coverage` ... with this text".** This fixes the content that users and validation see. A built-in held in a Rust constant, a bundled file or a generated table would show the same text, so the storage mechanism is discretionary.
- **"Only `{cite}` MAY reference this built-in" and the standard reference forms.** This is validation behavior: a role other than `{cite}` is reported. The clause names no required validator type, signature or delegation. The mechanism is left open.
- **"available in every project without a project requirement, site query, or exception-specific configuration".** This is observable availability. Registering the name globally or special-casing it in lookup both satisfy it.
- **The quoted built-in text.** It sets rules for authors and reviewers: when a coverage exception applies, what it excuses, and that an independent assessment must accept it. Other requirements enforce those rules, such as coverage checking and assessment. This requirement does not prescribe a type, field or library for them.
- **Contextual requirements.** `requirements.references.builtin_definitions` and `requirements.references.roles` supply context only. They describe how built-ins are resolved and displayed, and what each role means. The `requirements.references.source_item` definition is context only too.

Every clause therefore specifies only observable behavior, and no implementation evidence is needed.

behavioral: The subject has three observable obligations. The behaviors described inside the quoted text are the content of other requirements, so they need no test here.

1. **`habeas:coverage` exists with the stated text.** `src/builtins.rs#mod[tests]/fn[coverage_builtin_uses_the_documented_text_and_only_the_citation_role]` calls `builtin("habeas:coverage")`. It asserts that `text()` equals the block quoted in `md/reference.md` under "The built-in `habeas:coverage` has this text:". The `src/builtins.rs` `Builtin::text` snippet shows it reads the text from the quoted block in `md/requirements/test-coverage.md`, though the search output truncated that path. If so, the assertion also ties the built-in to the requirement text. It also spot-checks "difficulty alone", "file's 80%" and "without conditional build matching". It asserts that exactly one `BUILTINS` entry has this name.

2. **Only `{cite}` may reference it.** The same test asserts that `check(ReferenceKind::Cite)` is ok. It asserts that `check` returns an error for `Impl`, `Test`, `Fixme` and `Term`. Together these cover every other role. The `BUILTINS` entry lists only `Cite`. Validation reporting is owned by `requirements.references.builtin_definitions`.

3. **Available in every project without a declaration, site query or exception-specific configuration.** `src/lib.rs#mod[tests]/fn[fenced_references_render_their_badge_and_body_and_built_ins_are_unlinked]` builds a bare book from `book_root()` that declares nothing for `habeas:coverage`. It uses a fenced `:::{cite} habeas:coverage`, which is the standard fenced form. It asserts that the badge renders with hover text equal to the built-in's full text and has no link. It asserts no `href="habeas` appears. The inline form is exercised with `habeas:util` through the same resolution path. The role check does not depend on the form, so a separate inline `habeas:coverage` case adds nothing.

Both tests carry `{test}` markers for the subject, so there is no marking gap. I found no behavioral gap.

Only `{cite}` MAY reference this built-in, inline or fenced using the standard
reference forms of {cite}`requirements.references.roles`. The built-in MUST be
available in every project without a project requirement, site query, or
exception-specific configuration.
:::{req} builtin_definitions
Habeas provides built-in definitions named `habeas:<name>`, available in
every project without a declaration. Each built-in has fixed text, which
states its obligations and is documented in Habeas's reference documentation,
and states which reference roles may use it. References resolve built-in
names alongside project definitions. So that every book stands alone, a
built-in reference displayed under {cite}`requirements.references.book_badges`
uses a badge without a link whose hover text gives the built-in's full text.
Built-ins themselves neither require nor permit definition evidence files and
do not appear as definitions in the requirements index, `habeas status`, or the
missing-evidence check of
{cite}`requirements.ci.coverage`. Per-source citation reviews under
{cite}`requirements.references.citation_review` may be required for references
to a built-in. A project definition cannot use a full name beginning with
`habeas:`; validation reports one,
and the `:` character already makes such names invalid under
{cite}`requirements.ci.identifiers`. Validation reports a reference to a
built-in in a role the built-in does not permit, or that breaks the built-in's
stated form.
:::{req} roles

Project text files MAY use the `{impl}`, `{cite}`, and `{test}` roles with a backtick-delimited full requirement or example name, or with a built-in name under {cite}`requirements.references.builtin_definitions`, and MAY use the `{fixme}` role in fenced form. A reference MAY instead be written in fenced form, `:::{role} name` on one line, a body, and a closing fence, following the fence rules of {cite}`requirements.ci.span` and {cite}`requirements.ci.fence_lengths`; the fenced form is the same edge with attached commentary, and the inline form carries none. In a source comment, fence lines MUST be recognized after removing each line's comment delimiters within one comment run under {cite}`requirements.references.outline_comments`, and a fence that does not close within its comment run MUST be a validation error. Each reference is a directed edge between its source and the named definition. A source is a {term}`requirements.references.source_item` or a requirement or example declaration. The roles MUST mean:
- `{cite}`: the source relies on, supports, or refers to the definition. It is an
edge from the source to the definition.
- `{impl}`: the source implements part of the definition: it makes a decision,
performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case that the definition
specifies. A requirement MAY implement part of another requirement by refining
one of its obligations. Calling code that implements a definition, or
producing a result a caller uses to meet it, MUST NOT by itself count as
implementing it. A check MUST count only if the definition states it, or the
source could not meet one of the definition's obligations without it; source
that checks it is consistent with a definition, such as recognizing a form the
definition specifies in order to decide whether to run other behavior, relies
on that definition and calls for `{cite}`. A requirement stating a convention
for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by
the source that carries out the convention as a whole, such as the step that
collects and reports those outputs.
- `{test}`: the source is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies:
a test through its scenario and the assertions about that scenario's outcome,
or a named example through the concrete case it describes.
- `{fixme}`: the source acknowledges a known gap in fulfilling the definition. It
MUST use the fenced form, and its body MUST describe the gap. The body MAY
begin with option lines naming issues that track the gap, one per line, in the
form `:github: <owner>/<repo>#<number>`, such as
`:github: rust-lang/rust#123`. `github` MUST be the only recognized option.
A named `{fixme}` MAY appear only in sources outside the book. Validation MUST report
any other option line, a `:github:` value not in that form, an inline
`{fixme}`, a `{fixme}` in a requirement or example declaration, and a
`{fixme}` whose body, without option lines and comment delimiters, is empty.
An unnamed `{fixme}`, a fence of `:::{fixme}` with no name, MAY appear in any
project text, including a requirement or example body, to tie that place to
the issues it names. It MUST have at least one `:github:` option line and MAY
have a description; it is not a reference edge, acknowledges no gap, and needs
no evidence input. Its issues are checked under {cite}`requirements.cli.fixme_issues`.
`{impl}`, `{test}`, and `{fixme}` are edges from the definition to the source.
Code implementations are reviewed as part of the definitions they implement or
test. Citation reviews assess cited source items and book passages under
{cite}`requirements.references.citation_review`.
```text
{impl}`requirements.references.roles`
{cite}`requirements.references.roles`
{test}`requirements.references.roles`
:::{definition} source_item
:phrase: source item
A node in a project file’s outline, identified by the project-relative path
and an outline selector. For example, `src/auth.rs#fn[check_token]` identifies
a Rust function. The root node represents the whole file. A reference in a
comment belongs to the item that owns the comment under
{cite}`requirements.references.outline_comments`.
